passage: The cartoon ended and Kamal turned to the kitchen. "Mummy, one more show?" Rukmini looked up from the dal. "No, beta. It's bedtime soon, and tomorrow you can watch another." Kamal's lip stuck out and he grumbled, "Always no." But he stood up and dragged his feet to the bathroom anyway. She always tells me why, he thought. When Rukmini came to tuck him in, he held her hand and yawned. 🙂

qa.q: What did Kamal ask Rukmini for?
Why did Kamal go to the bathroom even though he grumbled?
qa.a: He trusts that his mother has a good reason, since she always tells him why. His grumbling was small.

qa.q: What makes Rukmini's no work well for a child like Kamal?
qa.a: It is kind and consistent, with a reason and a promise for tomorrow. Over time that helps Kamal accept rules without a fight. 😊

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel when Kamal grumbles but goes anyway?
qa.a: She is probably a little amused and relieved that he accepts it. She may also feel encouraged that her steady rule is working.

grounding: I ask for one more show and hear no; I grumble but trust my parent has a good reason.

Monday: "One more show, Mumma?" Zubin asked. "No, it's bath time." Zubin groaned and dragged his feet to the bathroom, grumbling the whole way.
Wednesday: "One more?" "Not tonight. Bath, then two stories." Zubin sighed, but he switched off the screen himself.
Sunday: Before Swati could say anything, Zubin clicked off the show. "Bath, then stories, right?" "Right," said Swati. Zubin stretched. "You always say no, but it's okay. Bath is warm anyway."

qa.q: What did Swati promise after the bath on Wednesday?
qa.a: She said bath, then two stories.

qa.q: What does Zubin switching off the show himself suggest he feels?
qa.a: He still feels a little grumpy, but he trusts that his mother's no is fair and that stories will come.

qa.q: Which part of Swati's approach built Zubin's trust?
qa.a: She gave the same kind no every night with a clear next step, so the rule felt steady instead of random.

qa.q: How might Swati feel on Sunday when Zubin switches off the show first?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and happy that the routine is working without a fight. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a child grumbles at a parent's no to more screen time but comes to trust and accept the rule.

passage: The power had gone out twice that evening, and the phone's battery was low. "One more show, Papa? Please?" Yamini begged. Ramesh shook his head. "No, kanna. We need the battery in case the lights stay off." Yamini pouted and crossed her arms. "Hmph." She kicked her pillow. Then she looked at Papa's face in the candlelight. Papa always had a reason. "Okay," she grumbled. "Can we make shadow animals instead?" Ramesh held up his hands and made a wobbly dog on the wall. Yamini giggled.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh want to save the phone battery?
qa.a: He said they needed the battery in case the lights stayed off.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she kicked her pillow?
qa.a: She felt cross and disappointed, but she still trusted that Papa had a reason.

qa.q: How could a parent make a no easier to trust, like Ramesh did?
qa.a: Give a short, kind reason and offer something else to do, such as shadow animals.

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh gave in because Yamini pouted?
qa.a: Yamini might learn that pouting works, and the battery could run out; the rule would feel less steady.

grounding: A child grumbles at a parent's no to another show but trusts there is a good reason and accepts it without a fight.
